title: Maitreyi's question
hookLine: offered her share of the property, Maitreyi asks the one question that makes the settlement worthless
tomorrow: "the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on"
last: A LIFE MOVES IN FOUR STAGES.

lines: WOULD THE WHOLE EARTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?
cards: Papers on the table. Everything divided, fair and square. Sign here.
And instead of signing, Maitreyi asks a question. Sir, if this whole earth, full of wealth, belonged to me, would that make me immortal? Yajnavalkya is an honest man.
No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich, but there's no hope of deathlessness through wealth. Then she says the line this day is named for.

teach.h: WHAT WOULD I DO WITH IT?
teach.b: What would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She doesn't refuse the money in a temper, and she doesn't make a speech about it.
She sees that the settlement answers the wrong question, and asks for the right one.
Notice the word she uses: amrita, deathless, the same word as the nectar the gods churned from the ocean. She wants the thing that doesn't end. Here's one of Hinduism's big maps of a life.
Tradition later named four aims: dharma, doing right; artha, wealth and security; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom from the round of death and birth. Wealth is a real aim, not a sin.
Maitreyi just sees it can't give the last one. And Yajnavalkya is delighted. You were always dear to me, he says, and now you say what's dear.
Come, sit. I'll explain it to you, and as I do, reflect on it. His first words are strange.
Truly, it is not for the husband's sake that a husband is dear. Not for the wife's sake that a wife is dear. Not for the sons' sake that sons are dear.
Not for wealth's sake that wealth is dear. And on: not for the gods' sake are the gods dear, not for all beings' sake are all beings dear. Today, stay with the first half, the not.
It isn't cold. Yajnavalkya is saying: look again. Something in the love isn't about them at all.
Tomorrow, the second half of the sentence, the part that says what love is for.

how: Maitreyi is remembered across Hindu tradition as a woman philosopher who chose knowledge over wealth; teachers of Vedanta often begin with her question when explaining why the Upanishads seek the self.

o: the wife who chose the deathless over wealth
a goddess of friendship and kindness
the wife who took the whole estate and left

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: the whole earth full of wealth
deathless; the nectar of the gods
freedom: the last of the four aims
the first half of his answer

s: Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi wealth will make her immortal
he says no: her life would be like the life of the rich, but wealth brings no hope of deathlessness.
Maitreyi asks him to teach her what he knows
what would I do with what won't make me immortal? tell me what you know.
Hindu teaching treats wealth as something sinful
artha, wealth, is one of the four aims of life. Maitreyi only sees it can't give the deathless.

games.q: you're Maitreyi. your husband is leaving, and he offers you a fair share of everything he owns. what do you do?
o: take the share and thank him.
ask whether all the wealth in the world would make you immortal.
games.why: she asks, and he answers honestly: no. so she sets the money aside: what would I do with what won't make me deathless? tell me what you know.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're chasing right now: money, a title, a house, being liked. Don't scold yourself; it's probably a fine thing, so just ask it her question, quietly: will you make me deathless?
Notice the honest answer, then ask what would, and let the question sit with you the way she sat down to listen.

wordCard.voice: Maitreyi. Offered her share of everything, she asks for amrita, the deathless, the one thing the whole earth full of wealth couldn't give her.

orig.note: Sanskrit amṛta: a (not) + mṛta (dead). deathless, and the nectar of immortality.

carryVoice: Your line: wealth can't buy the deathless. Tomorrow, a drum, a conch and a vina. Day three hundred sixty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (not for the husband's sake…)
